# Vector and matrix derivatives

<p class="chapter-kicker">Milestone 1 · Unit 4 · Completed 22 November 2026</p>

The scalar engine in unit 3 propagated derivatives by multiplying local rates and accumulating contributions from shared paths. The same reasoning applies when an operation consumes and produces entire vectors or matrices.

> How do we organize those local derivatives, and how do the resulting shapes determine a backward calculation?

::: {.callout-note title="Scope of this chapter"}
Seven exercises develop Jacobians as local linear maps and derive backward rules for matrix multiplication, shared parameters, bias broadcasting, elementwise activations, and sum and mean reductions. The final checkpoint combines those rules in a backward pass from a scalar loss to the inputs and parameters of a batched layer.
:::

## A Jacobian predicts local vector changes

In unit 1, a small displacement of a vector input changed a scalar output approximately by

$$
L(x+\Delta x)-L(x)\approx\nabla L(x)^\top\Delta x.
$$

Use **column vectors** throughout. Now let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ have components $f_1,\ldots,f_m$. Each component is a scalar function, so for a smooth $f$,

$$
\Delta f_i\approx\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}(x)\,\Delta x_j,
\qquad
\Delta f_i=f_i(x+\Delta x)-f_i(x).
$$

Stack these component equations. Their coefficients form the **Jacobian**:

$$
(J_f(x))_{ij}=\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}(x),
\qquad
\Delta f\approx J_f(x)\Delta x.
$$

For two inputs and two outputs,

$$
J_f(x)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1}&\dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_2}\\[5pt]
\dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_1}&\dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_2}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Every entry is evaluated at the same starting point $x$. The organization follows the matrix multiplication:

- **Row $i$** contains the derivatives of output $f_i$ with respect to the inputs.
- **Column $j$** describes the first-order response of every output to a change in input coordinate $x_j$ alone.

The general dimensions are

$$
\underbrace{\Delta f}_{m\times1}
\approx
\underbrace{J_f(x)}_{m\times n}
\underbrace{\Delta x}_{n\times1}.
$$

At a fixed $x$, multiplication by $J_f(x)$ is a linear map from input displacements to predicted output displacements. This is the derivative's **local linear map** interpretation. To predict the new output value, add the starting output:

$$
f(x+\Delta x)\approx f(x)+J_f(x)\Delta x.
$$

For a single scalar output $L$, the Jacobian has one row and equals $\nabla L(x)^\top$. The gradient itself remains a column.

### Exercise 1: predict two output changes

Take

$$
f(x_1,x_2)=\begin{pmatrix}x_1^2+x_2\\x_1x_2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
x=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Delta x=\begin{pmatrix}0.01\\-0.02\end{pmatrix}.
$$

1. Derive the symbolic Jacobian, then evaluate it at $(2,3)$.
2. Use the Jacobian to predict the output change.
3. Calculate the actual output change. Expand the component expressions to identify the terms omitted by the linear approximation.
4. Interpret the second column when only $x_2$ changes by a small amount $h$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: the Jacobian and its remainder"}
The four local derivatives give

$$
J_f(x_1,x_2)=\begin{pmatrix}2x_1&1\\x_2&x_1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
J_f(2,3)=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The predicted change is

$$
J_f(2,3)\Delta x
=\begin{pmatrix}4(0.01)-0.02\\3(0.01)+2(-0.02)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0.02\\-0.01\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The starting and new outputs are

$$
f(2,3)=\begin{pmatrix}7\\6\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
f(2.01,2.98)=\begin{pmatrix}7.0201\\5.9898\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus the actual change is $(0.0201,-0.0102)^\top$. Expanding before substituting numbers makes the discrepancy explicit:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta f_1
&=(x_1+\Delta x_1)^2+x_2+\Delta x_2-(x_1^2+x_2)\\
&=2x_1\Delta x_1+\Delta x_2+(\Delta x_1)^2,\\[4pt]
\Delta f_2
&=(x_1+\Delta x_1)(x_2+\Delta x_2)-x_1x_2\\
&=x_2\Delta x_1+x_1\Delta x_2+\Delta x_1\Delta x_2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The linear approximation omits the terms quadratic in the displacement. Actual change minus predicted change is therefore

$$
\begin{pmatrix}(\Delta x_1)^2\\\Delta x_1\Delta x_2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0.0001\\-0.0002\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The second Jacobian column is $(1,2)^\top$. A small change $h$ in $x_2$ alone gives the first-order output change $(h,2h)^\top$. In this particular example that change is exact for any $h$: with $x_1=2$ fixed, both output components are affine in $x_2$. Equivalently, both remainder terms vanish when $\Delta x_1=0$.
:::

## A scalar loss propagates backward through a Jacobian

The forward computation has three stages:

$$
\underbrace{x}_{n\times1}
\xrightarrow{\ f\ }
\underbrace{y}_{m\times1}
\xrightarrow{\ L\ }
\underbrace{L(y)}_{\text{scalar}}.
$$

We want the derivative of the final scalar loss with respect to the inputs of $f$. Writing $\nabla_xL$ is shorthand for the gradient of the composite function $L(f(x))$.

### Separate the local derivatives from the loss derivatives

Suppose the computation downstream of $y$ has already supplied

$$
g=\nabla_yL
=\begin{pmatrix}
\partial L/\partial y_1\\
\vdots\\
\partial L/\partial y_m
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This is the **incoming gradient** at the operation $f$ during the backward pass. There may be many more operations between $y$ and the loss; their effects are already summarized in $g$.

There are three different derivatives to keep track of:

| Derivative | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| $\partial y_i/\partial x_j$ | How does output $y_i$ of this operation respond to input $x_j$? |
| $g_i=\partial L/\partial y_i$ | How does the final loss respond to changing $y_i$, holding the other output coordinates fixed? |
| $\partial L/\partial x_j$ | How does the final loss respond to input $x_j$ through the complete computation? |

The Jacobian contains the first kind. The incoming gradient contains the second. The backward calculation combines them to obtain the third.

### Fix one input and collect its paths

Choose one input coordinate $x_j$. Keep $j$ fixed. Changing it may change several outputs, and each affected output provides a path to the loss:

$$
x_j\longrightarrow y_i\longrightarrow L.
$$

Along the path through $y_i$, multiply the two rates:

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}}_{\text{loss response}}
\underbrace{\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}}_{\text{local output response}}.
$$

Add those contributions over all outputs:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_j}
=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}
\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}.
$$

Here $j$ identifies the particular input derivative being calculated, while $i$ visits the outputs. The different letters distinguish their roles; their numerical values are allowed to coincide.

The sum follows directly from local changes. If only $x_j$ increases by a small amount $h$, then

$$
\Delta y_i\approx\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}h.
$$

The resulting loss change is, to first order,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta L
&\approx\sum_i g_i\Delta y_i\\
&\approx\left(\sum_i g_i\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}\right)h.
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $h$ is $\partial L/\partial x_j$. This is the same multiplication along paths and addition across paths used in the scalar engine.

### Why the Jacobian is transposed

Column $j$ of $J_f$ contains all the local derivatives needed for input $x_j$. Its dot product with $g$ gives one input-gradient component. For a two-input, two-output operation, write

$$
J_f=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
g=\begin{pmatrix}g_1\\g_2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The first input derivative uses the first column, $(a,c)^\top$; the second uses $(b,d)^\top$:

$$
\nabla_xL
=\begin{pmatrix}
ag_1+cg_2\\
bg_1+dg_2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Matrix–vector multiplication takes dot products with the matrix's rows. Transposing places those Jacobian columns into rows:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\b&d\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}g_1\\g_2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}ag_1+cg_2\\bg_1+dg_2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Collecting the component chain-rule sums therefore yields

$$
\boxed{\nabla_x L=J_f(x)^\top\nabla_y L.}
$$

The dimensions confirm the orientation:

$$
\underbrace{\nabla_x L}_{n\times1}
=\underbrace{J_f(x)^\top}_{n\times m}
\underbrace{\nabla_y L}_{m\times1}.
$$

### Obtain the same rule from local linear maps

For a general small input displacement, the forward derivative gives

$$
\Delta y\approx J_f(x)\Delta x.
$$

The incoming gradient predicts the loss change from that output displacement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta L
&\approx g^\top\Delta y\\
&\approx g^\top J_f(x)\Delta x\\
&=\bigl(J_f(x)^\top g\bigr)^\top\Delta x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Compare this with the defining local-change formula
$\Delta L\approx(\nabla_xL)^\top\Delta x$. The input gradient is the column of coefficients $J_f^\top g$.

The approximation is in predicting a finite change. The chain-rule identity for the derivatives at the chosen point is exact for differentiable operations.

Transposing the backward equation gives the equivalent row form,

$$
(\nabla_x L)^\top=(\nabla_y L)^\top J_f(x).
$$

The row-vector multiplication is a **vector–Jacobian product**, or **VJP**. Automatic differentiation also commonly uses this name for the equivalent column calculation $J_f^\top\nabla_y L$. Both expressions represent the same component chain-rule sums.

The Jacobian describes the local operation $f$. The incoming gradient describes how the chosen downstream loss responds to its outputs. Their product combines these two pieces, just as a scalar backward callback does.

### Exercise 2: propagate a scalar-loss gradient

Keep the function from exercise 1 and $x=(2,3)^\top$. Define

$$
y=f(x),\qquad L(y_1,y_2)=(y_1-1)^2+(y_2-2)^2.
$$

Calculate $y$ and $\nabla_y L$. Show both path contributions to each input derivative, then organize the result as a matrix product. Check the general dimensions for $n$ inputs and $m$ outputs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: path sums and the transpose"}
The forward value is $y=(7,6)^\top$, so

$$
\nabla_y L
=\begin{pmatrix}2(y_1-1)\\2(y_2-2)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}12\\8\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The input derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_1}&=12\cdot4+8\cdot3=72,\\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_2}&=12\cdot1+8\cdot2=28.
\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting these sums gives

$$
\nabla_x L
=\begin{pmatrix}4&3\\1&2\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}12\\8\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}72\\28\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The first row of this multiplication was the first column of $J_f$. This is why the backward rule uses the transpose. With $J_f$ of shape $m\times n$, its transpose maps an $m\times1$ output gradient to an $n\times1$ input gradient.

The same result in row form is

$$
(12\;8)\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}=(72\;28).
$$
:::

## A gradient with respect to a weight matrix

Consider one input column and one matrix multiplication:

$$
z=Ax,\qquad
A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad
x\in\mathbb R^{n\times1},\quad
z\in\mathbb R^{m\times1}.
$$

Componentwise, $z_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}x_j$. Holding $A$ fixed, $\partial z_i/\partial x_j=A_{ij}$, so the input Jacobian is $A$. Given an incoming gradient $g=\nabla_z L$, the input backward rule is

$$
\nabla_x L=A^\top g.
$$

Now hold $x$ fixed and differentiate with respect to the weights. A matrix stores many scalar weights; its loss gradient collects one derivative per entry:

$$
(\nabla_A L)_{ij}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial A_{ij}}.
$$

This gradient has the same shape as $A$. Changing only $A_{ij}$ directly affects only output $z_i$, at rate $x_j$. Consequently,

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial A_{ij}}=g_i x_j,
\qquad
\boxed{\nabla_A L=gx^\top.}
$$

This is an **outer product**:

$$
\underbrace{g}_{m\times1}
\underbrace{x^\top}_{1\times n}
=\underbrace{\nabla_A L}_{m\times n}.
$$

Every row of the gradient is the input row $x^\top$ scaled by the corresponding incoming sensitivity $g_i$.

### Exercise 3: calculate the input and weight gradients

Use

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&3&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
x=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
g=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The vector $g$ is supplied by an omitted downstream scalar-loss computation. Calculate $z$ and $\nabla_x L$. Derive each weight derivative from its affected output, calculate all six entries, and organize them into one matrix product with general dimensions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: an outer product of sensitivities and inputs"}
The forward output is

$$
z=Ax=\begin{pmatrix}2-2-1\\-3+1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The input gradient is

$$
\nabla_x L
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&3\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\-6\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For a weight $A_{ij}$, the single affected output gives

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial A_{ij}}
=\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i}\frac{\partial z_i}{\partial A_{ij}}
=g_i x_j.
$$

Thus the first gradient row is $4(2,-1,1)$ and the second is $-2(2,-1,1)$:

$$
\nabla_A L
=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix}(2\;-1\;1)
=\begin{pmatrix}8&-4&4\\-4&2&-2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For example, $A_{23}$ affects $z_2$ through the term $A_{23}x_3$, so its loss derivative is $g_2x_3=-2$. The output index comes from the weight's row; the input index comes from its column.

The general shape is $(m\times1)(1\times n)=m\times n$, matching the weight matrix.
:::

### Compute the backward product directly

Flattening the $mn$ weights into one vector would give a full Jacobian of the $m$ outputs with respect to those weights of shape $m\times(mn)$. Most of its entries are zero because a weight in one row directly affects only that row's output.

The outer product $gx^\top$ computes the contracted backward result directly in its natural $m\times n$ shape. This preserves the component chain rule while avoiding construction of the larger full Jacobian.

## Shared parameters collect contributions from every example

Use one weight matrix and one bias vector for two inputs:

$$
z^{(1)}=Ax^{(1)}+b,\qquad
z^{(2)}=Ax^{(2)}+b.
$$

The two expressions reference the same parameter entries. One scalar loss $L$ depends on both outputs and supplies $g^{(r)}=\nabla_{z^{(r)}}L$.

A shared weight has a path through each example:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial A_{ij}}
=g_i^{(1)}x_j^{(1)}+g_i^{(2)}x_j^{(2)}.
$$

The bias $b_i$ enters each $z_i^{(r)}$ with local derivative one, giving

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_i}=g_i^{(1)}+g_i^{(2)}.
$$

These are the same accumulation rules used for shared values in the scalar engine, now organized by parameter entries.

### Exercise 4: two examples share weights and bias

Keep the same $A$ and use

$$
x^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
g^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix},
$$

$$
x^{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
g^{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Show both example contributions to a weight derivative and a bias derivative. Calculate the complete matrix and bias gradients.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: add the shared-parameter contributions"}
The weight gradient is the sum of two outer products:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_A L
&=g^{(1)}(x^{(1)})^\top+g^{(2)}(x^{(2)})^\top\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}8&-4&4\\-4&2&-2\end{pmatrix}
+\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2&1\\3&6&-3\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}7&-6&5\\-1&8&-5\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the bias,

$$
\nabla_b L=g^{(1)}+g^{(2)}
=\begin{pmatrix}4-1\\-2+3\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Both incoming vectors are derivatives of the same chosen loss. Use them directly; any scaling from that loss's definition is already included in those derivatives.
:::

## Arrange the affine layer as a batch

Put $B$ examples into the rows of $X$. To preserve the same computation, define $W=A^\top$ and transpose the single-example equation:

$$
(z^{(r)})^\top=(x^{(r)})^\top W+b^\top.
$$

Keep the original bias $b$ as a column. Let $\mathbf1_B$ be the $B\times1$ column of ones. Stacking the output rows gives

$$
\boxed{Z=XW+\mathbf1_Bb^\top.}
$$

| Quantity | Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $X$ | $B\times n$ | Each row is an input transposed |
| $W=A^\top$ | $n\times m$ | Weights arranged for row inputs |
| $b$ | $m\times1$ | Shared bias column |
| $Z$ | $B\times m$ | Each row is an output transposed |
| $G=\nabla_Z L$ | $B\times m$ | $G_{ri}=\partial L/\partial Z_{ri}$ |

The product $\mathbf1_Bb^\top$ repeats the same bias row for every example. This is **bias broadcasting**, often abbreviated as $Z=XW+b$ when the repetition is implicit. The explicit expression fixes the orientation of the column bias used here.

### Derive the backward rules component by component

Start from

$$
Z_{ri}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{rj}W_{ji}+b_i.
$$

The indices have distinct roles: $r$ selects an example, $j$ an input coordinate, and $i$ an output coordinate.

**Weights.** A fixed weight $W_{ji}$ appears in output coordinate $i$ of every example. Its local derivative in row $r$ is $X_{rj}$, so

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{ji}}
=\sum_{r=1}^{B}G_{ri}X_{rj}
=(X^\top G)_{ji}.
$$

**Inputs.** A fixed input entry $X_{rj}$ affects every output coordinate in its own example row. The local derivative for output $i$ is $W_{ji}$:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X_{rj}}
=\sum_{i=1}^{m}G_{ri}W_{ji}
=(GW^\top)_{rj}.
$$

**Bias.** A fixed $b_i$ appears in column $i$ of every example row, each time with local derivative one:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_i}
=\sum_{r=1}^{B}G_{ri}
=(G^\top\mathbf1_B)_i.
$$

Collecting these results gives

$$
\boxed{\nabla_W L=X^\top G,\qquad
\nabla_X L=GW^\top,\qquad
\nabla_b L=G^\top\mathbf1_B.}
$$

Each gradient has the shape of its corresponding variable:

| Gradient | Product dimensions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| $\nabla_W L$ | $(n\times B)(B\times m)$ | $n\times m$ |
| $\nabla_X L$ | $(B\times m)(m\times n)$ | $B\times n$ |
| $\nabla_b L$ | $(m\times B)(B\times1)$ | $m\times1$ |

The component sums explain the transposes: each matrix product must collect contributions over the indicated index. The bias calculation sums **down each output column**, collecting the uses of one shared bias coordinate across the batch.

### Exercise 5: the batched affine backward pass

Use the same two examples in row form:

$$
X=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&1\\1&2&-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
W=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&3\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
G=\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

1. Derive all three backward rules from the component expression and identify their summation indices.
2. Express the results as matrix operations and check their general dimensions.
3. Calculate all three gradients. Compare the weight and bias results with exercise 4.
4. For $B=3$ and $m=2$, describe the output change $\Delta Z$ when only $b_2$ increases by $h$, holding inputs and weights fixed.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: batched products and the bias column sum"}
For the weights,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_W L
&=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\-1&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}7&-1\\-6&8\\5&-5\end{pmatrix}
=(\nabla_A L)^\top.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the inputs,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_X L
&=\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&3&1\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}4&2&-6\\-1&7&4\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first row agrees with the single-example input gradient from exercise 3.

For the bias, keep the established column convention:

$$
\nabla_b L
=\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf1_B^\top G=(3\;1)$ is the transpose of that bias gradient.

For three examples and two outputs, changing only $b_2$ by $h$ changes the entries $Z_{12},Z_{22},Z_{32}$:

$$
\Delta Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&h\\0&h\\0&h\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The output-coordinate index stays fixed at $i=2$ while the example index runs through all three rows. In the backward direction, those same uses of the shared bias contribute to one derivative, $\partial L/\partial b_2=\sum_{r=1}^{B}G_{r2}$.
:::

## Backward through an elementwise activation

After an affine layer, apply a nonlinear activation:

$$
Z=XW+\mathbf1_Bb^\top,
\qquad
H=\tanh(Z).
$$

Both $Z$ and $H$ have shape $B\times m$. Let the downstream scalar loss depend on $H$, possibly through additional operations. The forward and backward directions are

$$
Z\xrightarrow{\ \tanh\ }H\xrightarrow{\ \text{downstream computation}\ }L,
$$

$$
\underbrace{\nabla_ZL}_{\text{gradient we want}}
\ \longleftarrow\
\underbrace{\nabla_HL}_{\text{incoming gradient}}.
$$

We will call the incoming gradient $Q$:

$$
Q=\nabla_HL,
\qquad
Q_{ri}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial H_{ri}}.
$$

The letters distinguish where a loss derivative is measured. In the affine section, $G$ meant $\nabla_ZL$. Here $Q$ means $\nabla_HL$. The activation backward pass converts $Q$ into $G$, which can then be used in the affine rules already derived.

::: {.callout-note title="Read the calculation in three stages"}
First follow a single entry through the scalar chain rule. Then collect those entrywise equations into matrix notation. Finally compare that calculation with multiplication by the full Jacobian. Each stage describes the same derivatives with a different organization.
:::

### What does applying tanh to a matrix mean?

In this chapter, activation functions applied to matrices act **elementwise**. The notation

$$
H=\tanh(Z)
$$

is defined by

$$
H_{ri}=\tanh(Z_{ri})
\quad\text{for every }r,i.
$$

For example,

$$
\tanh\!\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
\tanh(a)&\tanh(b)\\
\tanh(c)&\tanh(d)
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This convention works for rectangular matrices and preserves their shape. Stating “tanh acts elementwise” makes the notation explicit.

Changing one entry of $Z$ changes the matching entry of $H$:

$$
Z_{ri}\longrightarrow H_{ri}=\tanh(Z_{ri}).
$$

Other activation entries use other input entries. This dependency structure is what makes the backward calculation simple.

### Follow one entry first

Fix an example row $r$ and an output coordinate $i$. For the displayed computation, the only path from $Z_{ri}$ into the downstream loss begins through $H_{ri}$. The scalar chain rule therefore gives

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{ri}}
=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial H_{ri}}
\frac{\partial H_{ri}}{\partial Z_{ri}}.
$$

Use the scalar derivative

$$
\frac{d}{dz}\tanh(z)=1-\tanh^2(z).
$$

The result is

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{ri}}
=Q_{ri}\bigl(1-\tanh^2(Z_{ri})\bigr).
$$

Because the forward pass has already calculated $H_{ri}=\tanh(Z_{ri})$, we can also write

$$
\boxed{
\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{ri}}
=Q_{ri}(1-H_{ri}^2).
}
$$

The three quantities have distinct meanings:

| Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $Q_{ri}=\partial L/\partial H_{ri}$ | Incoming loss sensitivity at the activation output |
| $1-H_{ri}^2$ | Local derivative of the activation at that entry |
| $\partial L/\partial Z_{ri}$ | Resulting loss sensitivity at the activation input |

The left-hand derivative is with respect to $Z_{ri}$ because we have propagated the loss derivative back across the activation. The derivative with respect to $H_{ri}$ is the incoming quantity on the right.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recall why the scalar derivative is 1 − tanh²(z)"}
Write

$$
a=e^z-e^{-z},
\qquad
b=e^z+e^{-z},
\qquad
\tanh(z)=\frac{a}{b}.
$$

Then $a'=b$ and $b'=a$. The quotient rule gives

$$
\frac{d}{dz}\frac{a}{b}
=\frac{a'b-ab'}{b^2}
=\frac{b^2-a^2}{b^2}
=1-\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^2
=1-\tanh^2(z).
$$
:::

### Where a sum over other entries would go

The one-term chain rule above is already valid. A general chain-rule sum is useful for making its dependency argument explicit.

When calculating $\partial L/\partial Z_{ri}$, $r$ and $i$ stay fixed: they identify the input entry whose loss derivative we want. To visit all activation outputs, introduce separate running indices $s$ and $j$:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{ri}}
=
\sum_{s=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{m}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial H_{sj}}
\frac{\partial H_{sj}}{\partial Z_{ri}}.
$$

The index roles are:

| Indices | Role in this calculation |
|---|---|
| $r,i$ | The fixed row and coordinate of the selected input $Z_{ri}$ |
| $s,j$ | Running indices visiting every output entry $H_{sj}$ |

Different letters do not require different values. One of the visited positions has $s=r$ and $j=i$.

For example, fix $Z_{12}$ in a $2\times2$ activation. The general sum visits

$$
H_{11},\quad H_{12},\quad H_{21},\quad H_{22}.
$$

Only $H_{12}$ changes when $Z_{12}$ changes. More generally,

$$
\frac{\partial H_{sj}}{\partial Z_{ri}}
=
\begin{cases}
1-H_{ri}^2,&s=r\text{ and }j=i,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

All but the matching term in the double sum vanish. This recovers exactly the direct one-term rule
$\partial L/\partial Z_{ri}=Q_{ri}(1-H_{ri}^2)$.

::: {.callout-note title="The loss can still combine different activation entries"}
Suppose, for example, $L=H_{11}H_{12}$. Then the incoming derivative at $H_{11}$ is $Q_{11}=H_{12}$. Changing $Z_{11}$ changes $H_{11}$, so

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{11}}
=H_{12}(1-H_{11}^2).
$$

The dependence of the loss on $H_{12}$ is already represented in the incoming derivative. There is no additional contribution through a change in $H_{12}$, because $H_{12}=\tanh(Z_{12})$ does not change when only $Z_{11}$ changes.

The local operation determines which intermediate entries a chosen input can affect. The incoming gradients summarize the remaining paths from those entries to the loss.
:::

### Why an affine input gradient has more terms

Compare the activation with the preceding affine layer:

$$
Z_{ri}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{rj}W_{ji}+b_i.
$$

Fix one input entry $X_{rj}$. It contributes to every output coordinate of example row $r$. With two output coordinates, the two paths give

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X_{rj}}
=
\underbrace{G_{r1}W_{j1}}_{\text{through }Z_{r1}}
+
\underbrace{G_{r2}W_{j2}}_{\text{through }Z_{r2}}.
$$

For $m$ output coordinates, the result is

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X_{rj}}
=\sum_{i=1}^{m}G_{ri}W_{ji}.
$$

That sum is built into the matrix product $\nabla_XL=GW^\top$. For a concrete check, use exercise 5's supplied $W$ and $G$. The input $X_{12}$ contributes to $Z_{11}$ with weight $W_{21}=2$ and to $Z_{12}$ with weight $W_{22}=3$:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X_{12}}
=G_{11}W_{21}+G_{12}W_{22}
=4\cdot2+(-2)\cdot3
=2.
$$

This agrees with the first row, second entry of the input gradient in that exercise.

| Local operation | Outputs affected by one input entry | Backward calculation |
|---|---|---|
| Elementwise activation | One matching activation output | One product |
| Affine layer, with respect to an input entry | Generally all output coordinates of the same example | Sum of products |

Both use the same chain rule. Their different local dependencies determine how many terms survive.

### Collect the scalar equations into matrix notation

We have one scalar equation at every position:

$$
(\nabla_ZL)_{ri}=Q_{ri}(1-H_{ri}^2).
$$

To collect these equations, define the **entrywise product**, also called the **Hadamard product**, by

$$
(U\odot V)_{ri}=U_{ri}V_{ri},
$$

for matrices $U,V$ of the same shape. This operation preserves that shape. In particular, $H\odot H$ squares each entry of $H$.

Let $\mathbf1_{B\times m}$ be the $B\times m$ matrix whose every entry is one. For the $2\times2$ example,

$$
\mathbf1_{2\times2}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The matrix rule is therefore

$$
\boxed{
\nabla_ZL
=Q\odot\bigl(\mathbf1_{B\times m}-H\odot H\bigr).
}
$$

This is more than removing indices: the notation must preserve the scalar operations at matching positions. Writing $H\odot H$ explicitly identifies an entrywise square; an ordinary matrix product $HH$ would mix coordinates and would require a square $H$.

The dimensions are:

| Quantity | Shape | Entry at $(r,i)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $Q$ | $B\times m$ | $Q_{ri}$ |
| $H\odot H$ | $B\times m$ | $H_{ri}^2$ |
| $D=\mathbf1_{B\times m}-H\odot H$ | $B\times m$ | $1-H_{ri}^2$ |
| $\nabla_ZL=Q\odot D$ | $B\times m$ | $Q_{ri}(1-H_{ri}^2)$ |

The table $D$ stores the local activation slopes. The incoming sensitivity and local slope at each position are multiplied to give the loss sensitivity at the corresponding input.

### The full Jacobian is diagonal

To relate this to the general rule $\nabla_zL=J^\top\nabla_hL$, flatten $Z$ and $H$ into vectors in the **same row-by-row order**. For a $2\times2$ matrix, use

$$
z=\begin{pmatrix}Z_{11}\\Z_{12}\\Z_{21}\\Z_{22}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
h=\begin{pmatrix}H_{11}\\H_{12}\\H_{21}\\H_{22}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Rows of the Jacobian correspond to entries of $h$; columns correspond to entries of $z$. Since each activation output depends on its matching input only,

$$
J=\frac{\partial h}{\partial z}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
D_{11}&0&0&0\\
0&D_{12}&0&0\\
0&0&D_{21}&0\\
0&0&0&D_{22}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The nonzero local derivatives are on the diagonal. Transposition leaves a diagonal matrix unchanged, so $J^\top=J$.

::: {.callout-note title="The table of slopes and the Jacobian have different shapes"}
$D$ is a $2\times2$ table with one slope per activation entry. The full Jacobian $J$ is a $4\times4$ matrix with one derivative for every output–input pair.

The four entries of $D$ supply the four diagonal entries of $J$. The remaining twelve Jacobian entries are zero because the corresponding output–input pairs have no dependency.
:::

### Diagonal multiplication is entrywise scaling

Flatten the incoming gradient in the same order:

$$
q=\begin{pmatrix}Q_{11}\\Q_{12}\\Q_{21}\\Q_{22}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Now write out the general backward product:

$$
J^\top q
=
\begin{pmatrix}
D_{11}&0&0&0\\
0&D_{12}&0&0\\
0&0&D_{21}&0\\
0&0&0&D_{22}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}Q_{11}\\Q_{12}\\Q_{21}\\Q_{22}\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
D_{11}Q_{11}\\
D_{12}Q_{12}\\
D_{21}Q_{21}\\
D_{22}Q_{22}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Each row has just one contributing term. Multiplying by this diagonal matrix scales each incoming-gradient entry by its matching local slope.

Those are exactly the products in $Q\odot D$. We can calculate them while retaining the original $B\times m$ layout:

$$
\text{flatten}(Q\odot D)=J^\top\text{flatten}(Q),
$$

where every flattening uses the same ordering.

This explains why the full Jacobian is unnecessary. The backward result is still the Jacobian–gradient product, but its known structure lets us calculate that product directly from the local slopes. We do not need to store its zero entries or flatten the matrices in the implementation.

For $N=Bm$ activation entries, an explicitly constructed full Jacobian has $N^2$ entries. Its diagonal has only $N$ local slopes. Once the slopes are known, applying the backward product needs just $N$ entrywise multiplications.

### Exercise 6: the elementwise tanh backward pass

Let $H=\tanh(Z)$, where $Z,H\in\mathbb R^{B\times m}$, and let $Q=\nabla_HL$ be the incoming gradient.

1. Derive $\partial L/\partial Z_{ri}$ from the component dependencies and the scalar derivative of tanh. If starting from a sum over all $H_{sj}$, explain which terms survive.
2. Express $\nabla_ZL$ using $Q,H$, a matrix of ones, and entrywise operations. Check the shapes.
3. Evaluate the rule for

$$
H=\begin{pmatrix}0&\tfrac12\\-\tfrac12&\tfrac45\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Q=\begin{pmatrix}2&-4\\3&5\end{pmatrix}.
$$

4. Describe the full $4\times4$ Jacobian for this example and explain why the backward result can be computed without constructing it.

The forward activation values are supplied. You do not need to recover $Z$ or evaluate hyperbolic functions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: scalar rule, matrix calculation, and diagonal product"}
For the selected entry $Z_{ri}$, only $H_{ri}$ changes. The scalar chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{ri}}
&=\frac{\partial L}{\partial H_{ri}}
\frac{\partial H_{ri}}{\partial Z_{ri}}\\
&=Q_{ri}\bigl(1-\tanh^2(Z_{ri})\bigr)\\
&=Q_{ri}(1-H_{ri}^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting all entries,

$$
\nabla_ZL
=Q\odot(\mathbf1_{B\times m}-H\odot H).
$$

Every matrix in the entrywise expression has shape $B\times m$, which is also the shape of $Z$.

For the supplied values, first calculate the entrywise squares:

$$
H\odot H
=\begin{pmatrix}
0^2&(\tfrac12)^2\\
(-\tfrac12)^2&(\tfrac45)^2
\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
0&\tfrac14\\
\tfrac14&\tfrac{16}{25}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Subtract from the matrix of ones to obtain the local slopes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D
&=\mathbf1_{2\times2}-H\odot H\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
-\begin{pmatrix}0&\tfrac14\\\tfrac14&\tfrac{16}{25}\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}1&\tfrac34\\\tfrac34&\tfrac9{25}\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply matching entries of the incoming gradient and local slopes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_ZL
&=Q\odot D\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}
2\cdot1&(-4)\cdot\tfrac34\\
3\cdot\tfrac34&5\cdot\tfrac9{25}
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}2&-3\\\tfrac94&\tfrac95\end{pmatrix}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For comparison, with row-by-row flattening the full Jacobian and incoming gradient give

$$
J^\top q
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0\\
0&\tfrac34&0&0\\
0&0&\tfrac34&0\\
0&0&0&\tfrac9{25}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\\3\\5\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\\tfrac94\\\tfrac95\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Reshaping this vector into two rows gives the same gradient matrix. Each row of the diagonal product uses only one local slope and its matching incoming-gradient entry. The entrywise calculation performs exactly those four products without storing the twelve zero entries of $J$.
:::

## Backward through a sum or mean

A batch of $B$ examples can produce one loss $\ell_r$ per example. A **reduction** combines these losses into a scalar. The sum and the mean over the batch are

$$
L_{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_{r=1}^{B}\ell_r,
\qquad
L_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{r=1}^{B}\ell_r,
\qquad B\geq 1.
$$

The forward pass combines $B$ losses into one value. The backward pass gives every loss entry its own partial derivative. To find the derivative for one entry, fix its index $i$ and vary just $\ell_i$ by $h$. The sum changes by $h$ because only one term in the sum changes. The mean changes by $h/B$ because the batch size stays fixed.

There is one coefficient per input entry. The sum gives every entry a coefficient of $1$, and the mean gives every entry a coefficient of $1/B$. These coefficients are constant because, for a fixed batch size, both reductions are linear in the loss vector.

### Exercise 7: reduce the batch and trace the gradient to a shared weight

1. Take $\boldsymbol{\ell}=(2,5,8)^\top$. Increase the middle loss from $5$ to $5.3$ and calculate the change in each reduction. Then increase it by a symbolic amount $h$ and derive the two partial derivatives with respect to $\ell_2$.
2. For a general batch size $B$, vary one arbitrary entry $\ell_i$. Write the two gradients with respect to the entire column $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ and give their shapes.
3. Suppose every $\ell_i$ depends on the same scalar weight $w$. Derive the two derivatives with respect to $w$. For $B=3$, evaluate them when the three local derivatives $d\ell_i/dw$ at the same $w$ are $2,-3,7$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: reduction gradients and shared-weight scaling"}
The original sum is $15$ and the original mean is $5$. With $\ell_2=5.3$, the sum becomes $15.3$ and the mean becomes $5.1$. The changes are $0.3$ and $0.1$, respectively.

For the symbolic change from $5$ to $5+h$, subtract the original values.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta L_{\mathrm{sum}}&=(15+h)-15=h,\\
\Delta L_{\mathrm{mean}}&=\frac{15+h}{3}-\frac{15}{3}=\frac{h}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Divide each change by $h\ne 0$. The quotients $1$ and $1/3$ are constant in $h$, so their limits as $h\to 0$ are the two partial derivatives with respect to $\ell_2$.

The same argument applies to any fixed entry $\ell_i$ of a batch of size $B$. The exact changes are $h$ and $h/B$, so

$$
\frac{\partial L_{\mathrm{sum}}}{\partial \ell_i}=1,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L_{\mathrm{mean}}}{\partial \ell_i}=\frac1B.
$$

Collecting the partial derivatives in the same order as the loss entries gives

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}L_{\mathrm{sum}}=\mathbf 1_B,
\qquad
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}L_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac1B\mathbf 1_B.
$$

Here $\mathbf 1_B$ is the column of $B$ ones. Both gradients have shape $B\times 1$.

When $w$ is shared, the chain rule adds one path through each $\ell_i(w)$. For a scalar objective $L$ formed by either reduction,

$$
\frac{dL}{dw}
=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \ell_i}
\frac{d\ell_i}{dw}.
$$

With the two sets of coefficients, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dL_{\mathrm{sum}}}{dw}
&=\sum_{i=1}^{B}1\cdot\frac{d\ell_i}{dw}
=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\frac{d\ell_i}{dw},\\
\frac{dL_{\mathrm{mean}}}{dw}
&=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\frac1B\frac{d\ell_i}{dw}
=\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\frac{d\ell_i}{dw}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the three derivatives $2,-3,7$, the sum gives $2-3+7=6$ and the mean gives $6/3=2$. Both calculations add the paths back to the same weight. The mean scales each path by $1/B$ at the reduction.
:::

## Unit checkpoint: combine the backward rules {#recorded-checkpoint}

The checkpoint uses a batched affine layer followed by entrywise tanh.

$$
Z=XW+\mathbf 1_B b^\top,\qquad H=\tanh(Z).
$$

The rows of $X$ are examples. Let $n$ be the number of input coordinates, $m$ the number of output coordinates, and $T$ a fixed target matrix.

| Quantity | Shape |
|---|---|
| Input $X$ | $B\times n$ |
| Weights $W$ | $n\times m$ |
| Shared bias $b$ | $m\times 1$ |
| Pre-activation $Z$, activation $H$, and target $T$ | $B\times m$ |
| Per-example loss column $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ | $B\times 1$ |
| Objective $L$ | Scalar |

For batch row $r$, sum the squared errors over the $m$ output coordinates and multiply by $1/2$. Average those per-example losses over the $B$ rows.

$$
\ell_r=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{m}(H_{rj}-T_{rj})^2,
\qquad
L=\frac1B\sum_{r=1}^{B}\ell_r.
$$

1. Derive $\partial L/\partial H_{ri}$ and $\partial L/\partial Z_{ri}$. Give the matrix forms $Q=\nabla_H L$ and $G=\nabla_Z L$, and check their shapes.
2. Starting with $G$, derive a component of each of $\nabla_X L$, $\nabla_W L$, and $\nabla_b L$. Write the matrix products, give their shapes, and explain which index each product sums over.
3. Take a batch with at least two examples and at least three output coordinates. For $\partial L/\partial X_{21}$, identify which entries of $G$ contribute. For $\partial L/\partial Z_{23}$, identify which entries of $Q$ contribute. Explain how the local dependencies let you compute these gradients without building full Jacobians.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution: a complete backward pass for one batched layer"}
#### From the batch loss to the activation

Fix row $r$ and output coordinate $i$. Within the list of per-example losses, only $\ell_r$ depends on $H_{ri}$. Within $\ell_r$, only the term with $j=i$ depends on that entry.

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{ri}
&=\frac{\partial L}{\partial H_{ri}}
=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \ell_r}
\frac{\partial \ell_r}{\partial H_{ri}}\\
&=\frac1B\cdot\frac12\cdot 2(H_{ri}-T_{ri})
=\frac{H_{ri}-T_{ri}}{B}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $1/B$ comes from the batch mean. The sum over output coordinates contributes a single squared-error term to this derivative. Collecting the entries gives

$$
Q=\frac{H-T}{B}\in\mathbb R^{B\times m}.
$$

#### From the activation to the affine output

Only $H_{ri}=\tanh(Z_{ri})$ depends on the selected $Z_{ri}$. Its local slope is $1-H_{ri}^2$, so

$$
G_{ri}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{ri}}=Q_{ri}(1-H_{ri}^2),
\qquad
G=Q\odot(\mathbf 1_{B\times m}-H\odot H)
\in\mathbb R^{B\times m}.
$$

Here $\odot$ denotes entrywise multiplication. The batch scaling is already present in $G$ through $Q$.

#### From the affine output to the inputs and parameters

In index notation the forward rule is $Z_{ri}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_{rk}W_{ki}+b_i$. Fix the entry being differentiated before choosing which index to sum over.

| Fixed entry | Entries of $Z$ that can change | Local derivative |
|---|---|---|
| $X_{rk}$ | Row $r$, with $i$ varying | $\partial Z_{ri}/\partial X_{rk}=W_{ki}$ |
| $W_{ki}$ | Column $i$, with $r$ varying | $\partial Z_{ri}/\partial W_{ki}=X_{rk}$ |
| $b_i$ | Column $i$, with $r$ varying | $\partial Z_{ri}/\partial b_i=1$ |

Multiply each local derivative by the matching entry of $G$ and add the contributing terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X_{rk}}
&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}G_{ri}W_{ki}
=(GW^\top)_{rk},\\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{ki}}
&=\sum_{r=1}^{B}X_{rk}G_{ri}
=(X^\top G)_{ki},\\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_i}
&=\sum_{r=1}^{B}G_{ri}
=(G^\top\mathbf 1_B)_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

- For $\nabla_X L=GW^\top$, row $r$ of $G$ pairs with row $k$ of $W$, which becomes column $k$ of $W^\top$. The inner axis runs over the $m$ outputs. The result has shape $B\times n$.
- For $\nabla_W L=X^\top G$, column $k$ of $X$ becomes row $k$ of $X^\top$ and pairs with column $i$ of $G$. The inner axis runs over the $B$ examples. The result has shape $n\times m$.
- For $\nabla_b L=G^\top\mathbf 1_B$, column $i$ of $G$ becomes row $i$ of $G^\top$ and pairs with the column of ones. This sums across the $B$ examples because every $Z_{ri}$ in that column uses the same $b_i$. The result has shape $m\times 1$.

#### Why the backward products can be computed directly

A full local Jacobian has a row for each output entry and a column for each input entry. The gradient for one input entry is the dot product of its Jacobian column with the incoming gradient, using the same output order for both.

For $X_{21}$, only $Z_{2i}$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$ can change. Their local derivatives are $W_{1i}$. The Jacobian column for $X_{21}$ is zero at every other output position, so the dot product reduces to

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X_{21}}
=\sum_{i=1}^{m}G_{2i}W_{1i}.
$$

This uses row 2 of $G$ and row 1 of $W$ directly. The matrix product $GW^\top$ evaluates the corresponding dot products for all input entries.

For $Z_{23}$ in the activation step, only $H_{23}$ can change. The Jacobian column has one potentially nonzero entry, so the dot product reduces to one multiplication.

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_{23}}=Q_{23}(1-H_{23}^2).
$$

The entrywise rule evaluates those multiplications for all positions. In both steps the backward computation evaluates the Jacobian–gradient product using the known local derivatives and their dependency pattern.
:::

The next unit uses these rules to implement the forward and backward passes of a small network in NumPy.
